1I (Number Theory)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Section I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
1I OurBigBook.com
Use the reduction algorithm for a positive definite binary quadratic form. A determinant-one shear (x,y)↦(x+ky,y) puts the middle coefficient in [−a,a]. If the resulting last coefficient is smaller than a, the determinant-one substitution (x,y)↦(−y,x) decreases the positive integer leading coefficient. Repeating terminates with a reduced positive definite binary quadratic form satisfying ∣b∣≤a≤c. These substitutions preserve proper equivalence of binary quadratic forms and the discriminant of a binary quadratic form.
The enumeration of reduced binary quadratic forms gives
163=4ac−b2≥3a2,1≤a≤7.
(1)
Since b2≡−163≡1(mod4), b is odd. For ∣b∣=1,3,5,7, the possible values of (b2+163)/4 are respectively 41,43,47,53. Each is a prime number greater than seven. But ac=(b2+163)/4, so its positive divisor a≤7 must be one. Then ∣b∣≤a forces b=±1 and c=41. The two signs are properly equivalent: substituting x↦x−y in x2+xy+41y2 gives x2−xy+41y2. Thus every form in question is properly equivalent to
x2+xy+41y2.​
(2)

The closed-set version of the Baire category theorem says that if a nonempty complete metric space X is a countable union X=⋃n=1∞​Fn​ of closed sets, then at least one Fn​ has nonempty interior. Equivalently, a nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed nowhere dense sets.

For each integer n≥0, put Zn​={z:f(n)(z)=0}. Every derivative f(n) is an entire function and cannot be identically zero: otherwise repeated integration would make f a polynomial. By the identity theorem for holomorphic functions, its zero set has empty interior, and continuity makes Zn​ a closed set. Thus Zn​ is nowhere dense.
The complex plane with its usual metric is a complete metric space, so the Baire category theorem gives z0​∈/⋃n≥0​Zn​. The Taylor series there has coefficients
n!f(n)(z0​)​=0for every n≥0.​

3G (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 172 Articles: 1
Section I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 172
3G OurBigBook.com
Each nonidentity element of the special orthogonal group SO(3) is a rotation fixing exactly the two unit vectors along its axis. Since G is a finite group, Ω is finite. If v∈Ω is fixed by g=1 and h∈G, then hv is fixed by hgh−1=1. Hence G acts on Ω by a group action.
Let N=∣G∣>1, let r be the number of orbits of a group action, and choose representatives with stabilizer subgroups of orders n1​,…,nr​, each at least two. Count pairs (g,v) with g=1 and gv=v. Counting by g gives 2(N−1). Counting by group orbits and using the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives
∑j=1r​nj​N​(nj​−1)=2(N−1),∑j=1r​(1−nj​1​)=2−N2​<2.
(4)
Every summand is at least 1/2, so r<4: there are at most three orbits. For the trivial group, Ω is empty and the assertion also holds.
For the rotation group of a regular dodecahedron, N=60. The three group orbits are the unit vectors towards the 12 face centres, 20 vertices and 30 edge midpoints, whose stabilizer subgroup orders are respectively 5,3,2. Rotations about these axes exhaust the nonidentity rotations. Consequently the orbit sizes are
12,20,30.​
(5)

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 159 Articles: 1
Section I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 159
4G OurBigBook.com
Use binary search: maintain the interval of possible integers and ask whether n is at least the first integer in its upper half. Each answer reduces the number of possibilities to at most its previous number divided by two, rounded up. After q questions at most ⌈106/2q⌉ possibilities remain. Since 220=1048576>106, twenty questions suffice.
A yes/no decision tree of depth twenty has at most 220 leaves, whereas the possible finishing orders number 15!=1307674368000. Thus twenty questions cannot identify the finishing order of fifteen horses, assuming no ties. With unrestricted yes/no questions, the exact minimum for n horses is ⌈log2​(n!)⌉: the leaf count is a lower bound, and repeatedly partitioning the remaining permutations into two nearly equal sets attains it. In particular fifteen horses require 41 questions.
By Stirling's formula,
log2​(n!)=nlog2​n−(log2​e)n+21​log2​(2πn)+O(n−1),​
(6)
so the leading number of questions is nlog2​n. These questions may ask about whole sets of possible orders; restricting them to pairwise comparisons is a different model.

Write u(y,θ)=∂θ​logf(y,θ) for the single-observation score function. Differentiating the normalization of the probability density function gives
Eθ​[u(Y,θ)]=∫f(y,θ)∂θ​logf(y,θ)dy=∂θ​∫f(y,θ)dy=0.
(7)
For discrete observations, use a sum instead. The allowed interchange of differentiation and integration is the usual regular-model assumption with common support. Adding these identities gives Eθ​Un​=0.
Let pθ​ be the joint density. Because T is an unbiased estimator with no explicit dependence on the parameter, differentiating Eθ​T=θ gives
1=∫T∂θ​pθ​=Eθ​[TUn​]=Covθ​(T,Un​).
(8)
The scores are independent random variables with mean zero, so variance additivity for independent random variables gives Varθ​(Un​)=nVarθ​(U1​). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the centred estimator and the score now gives the Cramér-Rao lower bound:
Varθ​(T)≥nVarθ​(U1​)1​.​
(9)
The denominator is the sample Fisher information. This bound concerns regular models with positive finite information; the preceding covariance identity explains why a small estimator variance requires a sufficiently informative score.

The equation is a conservation law nt​+Jx​=0 with diffusive flux J=−D(n0​/n)nx​. For positive density, insects move down the density gradient, with effective diffusion coefficient Dn0​/n: dispersal is stronger in low-density regions. This is logarithmic diffusion, since the equation is nt​=Dn0​(logn)xx​.
Put τ=Dt and ξ=x/τβ. A self-similar solution n=n0​τ−βg(ξ) conserves total number when ∫R​g=1. Its width shrinks to zero as t↓0; for an integrable nonnegative g, changing variables in the integral against a bounded continuous function proves convergence to n0​ times the Dirac delta distribution at the origin.
Substitution gives
−βτ−β−1(g+ξg′)=τ−2β(g′/g)′.
(10)
Matching powers for a nonstationary profile forces β=1. The profile equation integrates to g′/g=−ξg+C. For a centred even profile, C=0, and integration of g′=−ξg2 gives g=2/(ξ2+a2). Normalization requires 2π/a=1, hence
g(ξ)=ξ2+4π22​,n(x,t)=x2+4π2D2t22n0​Dt​.​
(11)
This is n0​ times a Cauchy distribution density with scale 2πDt. It is positive, has total mass n0​, and directly satisfies the nonlinear diffusion equation for t>0.

The fixed points are (0,0) and (±∣μ∣,μ2). The Jacobian matrix is
J(x,y)=(μ2−y2x​−x−1​).
(12)
At the origin its eigenvalues are μ2 and −1, so it is a saddle equilibrium for every allowed μ. At either nonzero fixed point the characteristic polynomial is λ2+λ+2μ2, giving
λ±​=2−1±1−8μ2​​.​
(13)
Thus both are stable nodes for 0<∣μ∣<1/(22​) and stable focuses for ∣μ∣>1/(22​). At equality the repeated eigenvalue is −1/2 and the matrix is not scalar, so there is only one independent eigenvector: the fixed point is a stable improper node.
The stable manifold of the origin is x=0, exactly: there y˙​=−y. Conversely, a trajectory converging to the origin with x=0 would eventually have x˙/x=μ2−y>μ2/2, which precludes convergence of x to zero.
For the local unstable manifold, write y=h(x)=ax2+bx4+O(x6). Reflection symmetry makes h even, and the invariance equation for a graph requires
h′(x)x(μ2−h(x))=−h(x)+x2.
(14)
Comparing quadratic and quartic terms gives 2aμ2=1−a and 4bμ2−2a2=−b. Therefore
y=1+2μ2x2​+(1+4μ2)(1+2μ2)22x4​+O(x6).​

The canonical momentum is pi​=∂L/∂x˙i​=mx˙i​+qAi​. Its time derivative contains the total derivative along the trajectory: p˙​i​=mx¨i​+q∂t​Ai​+qx˙j​∂j​Ai​. The Euler-Lagrange equation therefore gives
mx¨i​=q[−∂i​ϕ−∂t​Ai​+x˙j​(∂i​Aj​−∂j​Ai​)].

The specified vector potential gives B=(0,0,B). Put ω=qB/m, retaining its sign. The Lorentz force law yields x¨=ωy˙​, y¨​=−ωx˙ and z¨=0. For initial velocities (u,v,w) and ω=0, integration gives
x(t)y(t)z(t)​=x0​+ωu​sinωt+ωv​(1−cosωt),=y0​+ωv​sinωt−ωu​(1−cosωt),=z0​+wt.​​
(20)
The transverse motion is a circle centred at (x0​+v/ω,y0​−u/ω) with radius u2+v2​/∣ω∣. Thus the full orbit is a helix around a line parallel to the magnetic field, with period 2π/∣ω∣ and signed axial advance 2πw/∣ω∣ per turn. The charge sign determines the sense of rotation. If w=0 it is a circle, if u=v=0 it is a straight line parallel to the field, and if qB=0 all motion is uniform rectilinear motion.

10E OurBigBook.com
For neighbouring comoving observers separated by a small physical distance dℓ, the recession velocity is H(t)dℓ, where H=a˙/a is the Hubble parameter. During the photon's travel time dt=dℓ/c, the local Doppler effect gives dλ/λ=Hdt. Integrating along the ray gives the cosmological wavelength-redshift relation:
logλe​λ0​​=∫te​t0​​aa˙​dt,1+z=a(te​)a(t0​)​.​
(21)
The same ratio stretches the arrival interval of successive wave crests and of successive emitted pulses: dt0​=(1+z)dte​. Each photon loses a factor 1+z in energy because E=hc/λ. Thus energy arriving through the sphere per unit observer time has one factor from cosmological redshift and one from time dilation:
dt0​dE0​​=(1+z)2L​.​
(22)
This is the total power crossing the sphere; division by its area would give the observed flux.

11G (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 322 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 322
11G OurBigBook.com
Identify the Möbius group with PSL2​(C), the orientation-preserving isometry group of three-dimensional hyperbolic space. Here a properly discontinuous group action permits finite stabilizers: for each compact set K, only finitely many g satisfy gK∩K=∅.
Fix o∈H3. The set of isometries with d(o,go)≤R is compact. To see this, an orientation-preserving isometry is uniquely determined by the image of an oriented orthonormal frame at o. The image point lies in a compact closed hyperbolic ball and its frame lies in a compact rotation-group fiber. These choices parametrize the indicated set of isometries continuously.
A discrete subgroup of a topological group is closed: otherwise distinct subgroup elements accumulating at the same point would have quotients tending to the identity, contradicting isolation of the identity. Its intersection with a compact set is therefore finite. If K⊆B(o,R) and gK∩K=∅, choosing x,gx∈K gives d(o,go)≤d(o,gx)+d(gx,go)≤2R. Hence discreteness implies a properly discontinuous group action. Conversely, if the subgroup is not discrete, distinct gn​ tend to the identity. For a compact ball K with o in its interior, eventually gn​o∈K, so infinitely many gn​K meet K, contradicting proper discontinuity. This proves the equivalence.
Matrices of determinant one over the Gaussian integers are closed under multiplication and inversion, with inverse (d−c​−ba​). Quotienting by {±I} gives the specified group of Möbius transformations. The Gaussian integers form a discrete set in the complex plane, so these matrices form a discrete subgroup of SL2​(C), and the finite quotient remains discrete. Thus this group acts properly discontinuously on H3.
Explicit representatives of all four types are
typeellipticparabolichyperbolicloxodromic​matrix(01​−10​)(10​11​)(21​11​)(1+ii​11​)​trace0232+i​​​
(23)
The first is z↦−1/z and has order two; the second is the nonidentity translation z↦z+1. The third has positive real reciprocal eigenvalues (3±5​)/2, giving translation along an axis without rotation. For the last, a nonreal trace excludes both unit-modulus and real eigenvalues. Its multiplier therefore has modulus different from one and a nonzero rotation angle: it is a loxodromic Möbius transformation.

12G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 402 Articles: 1
Section II OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 402
12G OurBigBook.com
Use the square-root encryption convention called the Rabin-Williams scheme in the Cambridge course notes. Choose distinct large primes p,q≡3(mod4), keep them secret, and publish N=pq. A message block m∈{0,…,N−1} is encrypted as
c=m2(modN).​
(24)
Usually require gcd(m,N)=1; otherwise the message itself reveals a factor. For a quadratic residue c modulo p, Euler criterion gives c(p−1)/2=1, so c(p+1)/4 is a square root. Compute both signs modulo each prime, then combine the four sign choices by the Chinese remainder theorem. For a unit ciphertext there are four roots modulo N. Message redundancy identifies the intended root; squaring alone does not identify it uniquely.
To reduce integer factorization to recovery of square roots, choose x uniformly from (Z/NZ)×, compute c=x2, and ask the alleged decoder for any root y of c. Conditional on c, the secret x is uniform among its four roots, even if the decoder deterministically chooses y. With probability 1/2, y≡±x(modN). Then the signs agree modulo one prime and disagree modulo the other. Since
N∣(x−y)(x+y),1<gcd(x−y,N)<N,​
(25)
the greatest common divisor factors N. Independent trials require an expected two successful oracle calls. If a trial's chosen x is not a unit, gcd(x,N) already factors N. This establishes the computational equivalence between factorization and inversion of the squaring map; it does not claim that learning any partial information about a formatted message is equivalent to full inversion.
For coin flipping by telephone, Alice publishes N with its factorization secret. Bob chooses uniformly a unit x with 0<x<N/2 and sends c=x2modN. Alice computes the two roots r1​,r2​ in this half interval, selects a binary digit in which they differ, and announces a guess for that digit of Bob's x. Bob reveals x; Alice verifies its range and square, and their common bit records whether her guess was correct. Alice then reveals p,q, so Bob verifies the primes, product, and differing digit.
Conditional on c, Bob's original root is equally likely to be r1​ or r2​, so Alice's guess succeeds with probability 1/2. Bob cannot change his answer to the other half-interval root without finding a nontrivial second square root, which would factor N by the argument above. Thus, assuming factorization is hard and the prescribed sampling and completed exchange are followed,
P(Alice wins)=P(Bob wins)=21​.​
(26)
The revealed factors make the completed transcript checkable. The protocol does not prevent a party from aborting communication.

13J OurBigBook.com
Use a normal linear model
Ti​=β0​+β1​di​+β2​hi​+εi​,εi​∼iidN(0,σ2).
(27)
The distance and climb are treated as fixed predictors; the assumptions are a linear conditional mean, independent errors with common variance, and normal errors for the exact tests. Fit by ordinary least squares using
hills.lm1 <- lm(time ~ dist + climb, data = hills)
The overall null hypothesis is β1​=β2​=0, against at least one nonzero slope. The intercept-only and full models have respectively 34 and 32 residual degrees of freedom. Under the null, the F-test statistic is
F=RSS1​/32(RSS0​−RSS1​)/2​≃181.66∼F2,32​.
(28)
The displayed residual sums are rounded; use the reported statistic for the test. Its upper-tail p-value is below 2.2×10−16, so reject the no-relationship hypothesis overwhelmingly. At least one predictor adds information beyond a constant mean.
In the coefficient table, Estimate gives one of the ordinary least squares estimators, Std. Error is the estimated standard deviation of that estimator, t value is the estimate divided by its standard error, and the last column is the two-sided p-value for a zero coefficient. Under the corresponding null, the statistic has a Student's t-distribution with 32 degrees of freedom. The fitted mean is
T=−8.992039+6.217956d+0.011048h.​
(29)
At fixed climb, an extra mile predicts about 6.22 extra minutes; at fixed distance, an extra foot of climb predicts about 0.01105 extra minutes. Both slopes have strong evidence of being positive. Specifically the climb test uses t=5.387 and p=6.45×10−6, so climb remains significant after controlling for distance. The intercept differs from zero at the 5% level, but extrapolating to a zero-distance, zero-climb race has no useful physical interpretation.
The regression diagnostics show a very large positive residual for Knock Hill and a smaller positive outlier for Bens of Jura. The Q-Q plot has a pronounced upper tail, contradicting the assumed normal-error pattern. These observations can distort both the fitted coefficients and the estimated error variance. Check the source records, units, transcription and any unusual race conditions first, especially for Knock Hill; correct a demonstrated data error and refit. If the records are valid, consider omitted terrain effects, nonlinear distance/climb effects, a suitable response transformation or robust regression, and compare fits with and without influential observations. A diagnostic outlier alone is not a reason to silently delete a valid record.

Extend q by zero to x<0 and apply the assumed Fourier inversion theorem. For sufficiently regular, decaying data and x>0 this gives q(x)=(2π)−1∫R​eikxq​(k)dk, with q​(k)=∫0∞​e−ikxq(x)dx. If Imk≤0, the exponential in this last integral is bounded in magnitude by one; it defines a holomorphic transform in the lower half-plane, with its boundary values on the real axis.
The PDF orients L from i∞ down to zero, then from zero to +∞. The function eikxq​(−k) is holomorphic in the upper half-plane, and for x>0 its exponential decays there. Close the two rays through a large first-quadrant arc. Cauchy integral theorem and Jordan lemma give
∫L​eikxq​(−k)dk=0.​
(30)
For example, if q,q′ are integrable, integration by parts gives q​(−k)=O(1/k) in that quadrant, which suffices for the arc estimate. Standard limiting arguments extend the identity to the admissible Fourier-inversion class. Adding any constant multiple of this zero integral to ordinary inversion proves
q(x)=2π1​∫R​eikxq​(k)dk+2πc​∫L​eikxq​(−k)dk,c∈C.​
(31)
The extra integral is a reflected, zero-supported contribution, not an extra datum.

The inductive definition of ordinal addition is α+0=α, α+(β+1)=(α+β)+1, and α+λ=supβ<λ​(α+β) for a nonzero limit ordinal λ. The synthetic definition is the order type of the order sum obtained by putting a copy of β after a disjoint copy of α.
These agree by transfinite induction on the second argument. Appending no points gives α; appending one new greatest point gives a successor. At a limit stage, the order sum is exhausted by the increasing initial segments obtained by appending each β<λ, so its order type is their supremum. Thus the synthetic construction satisfies all three recursion clauses, and uniqueness of transfinite recursion proves equivalence.

17F (Graph Theory)

Words: 281 Articles: 1
Section II OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 281
17F OurBigBook.com
A matching in a graph is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. A matching from X to Y here covers every vertex of X. Necessity of the Hall marriage theorem condition is immediate: the partners of vertices of A⊆X are distinct members of its neighbour set Γ(A).
For sufficiency, take a matching of maximum size. If it leaves x∈X unmatched, follow alternating unmatched and matched edges from x. Let A⊆X and B⊆Y be the reachable vertices. No vertex of B can be unmatched, because the resulting augmenting path in a matching would increase the matching. Every neighbour of A is in B, and the matching pairs B bijectively with A∖{x}. Thus ∣Γ(A)∣=∣B∣=∣A∣−1, contradicting Hall's condition. The maximum matching therefore covers X.
For the deficiency bound, adjoin d new vertices to Y, each adjacent to all of X. Every nonempty A then has ∣Γ(A)∣+d≥∣A∣ neighbours. Apply the Hall marriage theorem and remove the at most d edges using new vertices. This leaves at least ∣X∣−d independent edges. The lower bound is vacuous if d>∣X∣.
Write the adjacency matrix of a graph in bipartite block form (0CT​C0​). If Hall's condition failed for A⊆X, the linear map from vectors supported on A to their neighbour coordinates in Y would have fewer output than input coordinates. It therefore has a nonzero kernel, giving a nonzero vector v supported on A with CTv=0. The vector (v,0) would be a zero eigenvector of the adjacency matrix. Consequently absence of the zero eigenvalue implies a matching covering X.
The converse is false, even with equal part sizes. The four-cycle K2,2​ has a perfect matching, but its matrix C=(11​11​) is singular. Its adjacency matrix has eigenvalues 2,−2,0,0.

i OurBigBook.com
A field homomorphism fixing K is injective, since its kernel is an ideal of a field and cannot contain one. It is also K-linear. Equal finite field extension degrees then make it a bijection, hence a K-isomorphism.
Equal degrees alone do not ensure that any such homomorphism exists. For example Q(2​) and Q(3​) both have degree two, but a Q-isomorphism would require a square root of two in Q(3​). Squaring a+b3​ with rational a,b would give 2ab=0 and a2+3b2=2. Neither a2=2 nor b2=2/3 has a rational solution. Thus the two degree-two extensions are not isomorphic over Q.

An isomorphism fixing L fixes its subfield K, so an L-isomorphism is a K-isomorphism. The converse is false because an isomorphism over K may act nontrivially on L.
Take K=Q, L=Q(2​), α=21/4>0, F=L(α) and F′=L(iα). Both are degree-two extensions of L. The polynomial X4−2 is irreducible over Q by the Eisenstein criterion, and both α and iα are roots. Sending α to iα therefore gives a Q-isomorphism F→F′; on L it sends 2​ to −2​.
There is no L-isomorphism. The two quadratic extensions adjoin square roots of 2​ and −2​. Their square classes would agree only if −1 were a square in L. To check this criterion directly, a square root of 2​ in L(iα) would have form a+b(iα); its square forces ab=0. The case b=0 would put α in L, while a=0 would require b2=−1. Both are impossible, the latter since L⊆R. Thus the extensions are isomorphic over K but not over L.

For the order-18 group, the index-two subgroup P is normal and G=⟨P,t⟩. Restrict a complex irreducible representation V to the finite abelian group P. Simultaneous diagonalization decomposes it into character spaces Vχ​. The inversion relation makes t exchange Vχ​ and Vχ−1​. The sum of spaces belonging to any such character orbit is G-invariant, so irreducibility leaves only one orbit.
If the character is trivial, all of P is in the representation's kernel. Otherwise χ has order three and χ=χ−1. The only spaces are Vχ​ and Vχ−1​, and both have the same kernel in P. The prime two ramifies as (2)=p22​, where p2​=(2,1+s). Three splits as (3)=p3​p​3​, choosing p3​=(3,1+s), whereas five is inert because −17≡3(mod5) is not a square. The norm bound therefore leaves only the classes of 1, p2​, p3​ and p​3​; a norm-four ideal is p22​ and is principal.
The ideal p2​ is not principal, since an element of norm two would solve a2+17b2=2. On the other hand N(1+s)=18, and 1+s is divisible by p2​ and p3​ but not p​3​. Unique prime ideal factorization and the norm give (1+s)=p2​p32​. Thus [p3​]2=[p2​], which has order two, and
Cl(Q(−17​))≅C4​.​

For the Diophantine equation, x must be positive. If x were even, y2≡15(mod32), impossible for a square. Thus x is odd and y even. If 17∣x, then 17∣y, but y2+17 would have 17-adic valuation one while x5 has valuation divisible by five, also impossible.
The ideals (y+s) and (y−s) are consequently coprime. A common prime divides 2s and hence lies over two or seventeen, both excluded above. Their product is (x)5, so unique prime ideal factorization gives (y+s)=a5. Since the ideal class group has order four, [a]5=1 forces [a]=1. Write a=(a+bs) with integers a,b. The only units are ±1 by their norm, and the sign can be absorbed into the fifth power. Hence y+s=(a+bs)5.
Comparing the coefficient of s gives
1=b(5a4−170a2b2+289b4),b=±1.

For b=1, the bracket would be one, but it is four modulo five. For b=−1, the bracket would be minus one, but it is one modulo three for either possible square residue of a. Both cases are impossible. Therefore there are no integer solutions.

The real Stone-Weierstrass theorem says that a subalgebra of C(X,R) on a compact metric space is uniformly dense if it contains the constants and separates points. The finite sums ∑i​fi​(x)gi​(y) form such an algebra on [0,1]2: multiplication preserves this form, the constant one belongs to it, and the coordinate functions distinguish every pair of different points. Thus they approximate the continuous kernel uniformly.
A finite-rank operator has finite-dimensional range. A compact operator maps the unit ball to a set with compact closure, equivalently sends every bounded sequence to a sequence with a convergent subsequence. The identity on C[0,1] is bounded but not compact: the functions xn have supremum norm one, and every subsequence has the discontinuous pointwise limit which is zero on [0,1) and one at one. It therefore has no uniformly convergent subsequence.
A bounded finite-rank operator is compact because bounded sets in its finite-dimensional range have compact closure. Suppose Tn​→T in operator norm. For any ε>0, choose n with ∥T−Tn​∥<ε/3 and a finite ε/3-net for Tn​ of the unit ball. The same centres give an ε-net for T of that ball. Its closure is totally bounded and complete in the Banach space Y, hence compact. Thus an operator-norm limit of compact operators is compact.
For Kn​(x,y)=∑i​fi​(x)gi​(y) uniformly approximating K, the integral operator Tn​ has range in span{fi​} and is bounded. Moreover
∥(T−Tn​)f∥∞​≤∥K−Kn​∥∞​∥f∥∞​.
(56)
Consequently Tn​→T in operator norm, proving that the stated integral operator is compact.

23G (Riemann Surfaces)

Words: 260 Articles: 1
Section II OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 260
23G OurBigBook.com
Near an isolated point P∈A, choose source and target coordinate charts, using continuity of α to keep a sufficiently small source neighbourhood in the target chart. The coordinate representation is holomorphic on the punctured neighbourhood and is bounded near P by continuity. The Riemann removable singularity theorem extends it holomorphically across P, with the given continuous value. Repeating at all points of A proves that α is analytic.
For a nonconstant holomorphic function f on a connected Riemann surface, let A be the set where its coordinate derivative vanishes. This condition is independent of the chart. The derivative cannot vanish identically on an open set, because the identity theorem would then make f constant globally. Its zeros are isolated and closed locally, so A is a closed discrete subset. At every other point the holomorphic inverse function theorem makes f a local coordinate chart.
Now suppose α is a homeomorphism and g=f∘α is analytic. Outside α−1(A), use f as a target coordinate to write locally α=f−1∘g. This is analytic. The preimage α−1(A) is discrete because α is a homeomorphism, and the first argument extends analyticity across it. An injective holomorphic map cannot have a zero derivative: a zero of order at least two would give a locally multiple-to-one map. Its local inverse is therefore holomorphic, proving that α is a conformal equivalence.
The plane C and the unit disk are homeomorphic by z↦z/(1+∣z∣), with inverse w↦w/(1−∣w∣). They are not conformally equivalent: a holomorphic equivalence from the plane to the disk would be a bounded nonconstant entire function, contradicting Liouville's theorem.

A point x is critical for a smooth map f:X→Y when Dfx​:Tx​X→Tf(x)​Y is not surjective. A critical value is the image of a critical point; a regular value has no critical point in its fiber, including the case of an empty fiber.
To prove the regular level set theorem, take x0​∈f−1(y) and write n=dimX, m=dimY. In local coordinates, surjectivity supplies an invertible m×m derivative minor; relabel source coordinates so it uses the first m columns. The map
Φ(x)=(f1​(x),…,fm​(x),xm+1​,…,xn​)
(60)
has an invertible derivative. The inverse function theorem makes it a local diffeomorphism. In these coordinates the fiber is obtained by fixing its first m coordinates, so it is locally an open subset of Rn−m. These smooth charts prove that a nonempty regular fiber is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension n−m, with tangent space kerDfx​.
For the special orthogonal group, use F:Mn​(R)→Symn​(R) defined by F(A)=AAT. Its derivative is DFA​(H)=HAT+AHT. At an orthogonal A, any symmetric matrix B is obtained by taking H=BA/2, so I is a regular value. Therefore O(n)=F−1(I) has dimension n2−n(n+1)/2=n(n−1)/2. The determinant takes only the values ±1 there, so SO(n) is an open and closed part of O(n) and has the same manifold dimension:
dimSO(n)=2n(n−1)​.​

TA​SO(n)={H:AHT+HAT=0}={AK:KT=−K}.​
(62)
Thus its translated tangent space is the vector space of skew-symmetric matrices.

In phase-space coordinates z=(x,v), the characteristic equations for a transport equation are the Hamilton equations
X˙=∇v​H(X,V),V˙=−∇x​H(X,V),(X(0),V(0))=(ξ,η).

Smoothness of H gives a unique local Hamiltonian flow Φt​(ξ,η)=(X(t),V(t)). Along it the chain rule gives d[f(X,V,t)]/dt=0. Thus
f(x,v,t)=fI​(Φ−t​(x,v)).​
(92)
The inverse is the backward autonomous flow, so this formula defines the unique local classical solution wherever the characteristic reaches the initial hypersurface. A smooth Hamiltonian on all of R2n need not have a globally complete flow; the formula is understood on the interval and region where both flows exist. A common global time interval requires the corresponding completeness or growth assumption.

The microcanonical ensemble describes an isolated system at fixed energy, volume and particle number. The canonical ensemble describes fixed particle number and volume with heat exchange at a prescribed temperature. The grand canonical ensemble additionally allows particles to exchange with a reservoir, prescribing temperature, volume and chemical potential. Their respective equilibrium probabilities are uniform on the accessible energy shell, proportional to e−βEn​, and proportional to e−β(En​−μNn​). For stable short-range systems in the thermodynamic limit, concentration of relative energy and particle-number fluctuations and concavity of entropy make their bulk predictions equivalent; phase coexistence or nonadditive interactions require care.
For the microcanonical case restrict the allowed states to the fixed-energy shell of size Ω, imposing pn​=0 outside it. Maximize the Gibbs entropy subject to ∑pn​=1. A Lagrange multiplier gives −kB​(logpn​+1)+λ=0 on the shell, so
pn​=1/Ω on the shell,S=kB​logΩ.​
(116)
For the canonical case impose both normalization and ∑pn​En​=U. Stationarity of −kB​∑pn​logpn​−λ(∑pn​−1)−kB​β(∑pn​En​−U) gives pn​∝e−βEn​. Thus
pn​=e−βEn​/Z,Z=n∑​e−βEn​,β=(kB​T)−1.​
(117)
The last identification follows from ∂S/∂U=1/T. Entropy is strictly concave in the probabilities, so these stationary distributions are maxima.
For the independent three-level particles, put z=ϵ/(kB​T) and Z1​=1+2coshz. The full partition function is Z1N​ because the particles occupy labeled lattice sites. Differentiation gives
E=−1+2coshz2Nϵsinhz​,C=NkB​z2(1+2coshz)22coshz+4​.​
(118)
The heat capacity also equals NVar(E1​)/(kB​T2), confirming positivity. As T→+∞, the three occupations become equal:
E∼−3kB​T2Nϵ2​→0,C∼3kB​T22Nϵ2​→0.​
(119)
As T↓0, all particles occupy their unique lowest state:
E=−Nϵ+Nϵe−z+O(e−2z),C∼NkB​z2e−z→0.​
(120)
A negative temperature is possible because the total energy is bounded above. An equilibrated population inversion has more particles at +ϵ than at −ϵ. For example probabilities (p−​,p0​,p+​)=(1,2,4)/7 correspond to T=−ϵ/(kB​log2) and mean energy 3Nϵ/7. This is a macroscopic occupation pattern; an isolated individual microstate is not itself assigned a temperature. At the positive zero-temperature limit the ground state is unique, so the entropy tends to zero: the system obeys the third law of thermodynamics. The negative-temperature branch likewise approaches the unique highest-energy state as T→0−; it does not introduce residual ground-state entropy.

Hence magnetic fields penetrate only a surface layer of thickness λL​ and vanish deep in the macroscopic bulk, the Meissner effect. This conclusion uses the uniform-density, smooth-phase setting; a vortex has a singular phase and a nonuniform core and is outside those assumptions.

37D (General Relativity)

Words: 201 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 201
37D OurBigBook.com
Using the affine parameter and the normalization requested for the geodesic Lagrangian,
L=−2u˙v˙+x˙2+y˙​2−2H(u,x,y)u˙2.​
(126)
The coordinate v is cyclic. Its Euler-Lagrange equation gives u¨=0. The transverse coordinate equations give x¨+Hx​u˙2=0 and y¨​+Hy​u˙2=0. For the remaining coordinate,
∂u˙∂L​=−2v˙−4Hu˙,∂u∂L​=−2Hu​u˙2.
(127)
Its Euler-Lagrange equation, after using u¨=0, is
u¨=0,x¨+Hx​u˙2=0,y¨​+Hy​u˙2=0,v¨+2(Hx​x˙+Hy​y˙​)u˙+Hu​u˙2=0.​
(128)
Compare with x¨a+Γbca​x˙bx˙c=0. With indices (1,2,3,4)=(u,v,x,y), the complete list of nonzero Christoffel symbols, including symmetry of the lower indices, is
Γ112​=Hu​,Γ132​=Γ312​=Hx​,Γ142​=Γ412​=Hy​,Γ113​=Hx​,Γ114​=Hy​.​
(129)
All contracted symbols Γadd​ vanish. For R11​, the first derivative term in the supplied Ricci tensor formula is ∂v​Hu​+∂x​Hx​+∂y​Hy​=Hxx​+Hyy​, since H is independent of v. The second derivative term vanishes because the trace symbols vanish. The third term vanishes for the same reason, and every possible product in the last term requires a zero symbol with upper index 1 or a lower 2, so it also vanishes. Thus
Ruu​=Hxx​+Hyy​,Rab​=0 for the other components.​
(130)
The Vacuum Einstein equations with zero cosmological constant require Rab​=0, and therefore Hxx​+Hyy​=0​. The wave profile of this plane-fronted gravitational wave is harmonic in the transverse plane for each fixed u.

38B (Fluid Dynamics II)

Words: 239 Articles: 1
Section II OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 239
38B OurBigBook.com
The outer fluid is at rest, so its pressure is independent of x and dP/dx=0. Using incompressibility, the longitudinal boundary-layer equation becomes the conservative momentum equation
∂x​(ρu2)+∂y​(ρuv−μuy​)=0.
(131)
Integrating across the jet and using u,uy​→0 and uv→0 at both transverse infinities gives
dxdF​=0,F=ρ∫−∞∞​u2dy.​
(132)
Put ν=μ/ρ. The momentum-flux scaling gives U2δ∼F/ρ, while balancing longitudinal convection with transverse viscous diffusion gives U2/x∼νU/δ2. Eliminating U or δ yields
δ∝x2/3,U∝x−1/3.​
(133)
Choose the precise width convention Uδ2=νx and take U to be the centre-line velocity. For the self-similar solution with streamfunction ψ=Uδf(η), η=y/δ,
u=Uf′,v=3xUδ​(2ηf′−f),ux​=xU​(−3f′​−32ηf′′​).
(134)
The ηf′f′′ terms cancel in uux​+vuy​, leaving −U2[(f′)2+ff′′]/(3x). Since uyy​=Uf′′′/δ2, the dimensionless profile equation is
f′′′+31​(ff′′+(f′)2)=0.​
(135)
For a symmetric jet choose its streamfunction zero at the axis. The boundary and amplitude conditions are f(0)=0, f′′(0)=0, f′(0)=1, and f′(η)→0 as η→±∞, with f bounded and f′′→0. The momentum normalization is
F=ρU2δJ,J=∫−∞∞​[f′(η)]2dη.​
(136)
It determines the dimensional constants in U,δ; one should not independently impose J=1 after fixing both the centre-line and width conventions.
Indeed integrating the profile equation once and using its far-field conditions gives f′′+ff′/3=0. With the axis conditions, f′=1−f2/6, and therefore
f(η)=6​tanh(η/6​),f′(η)=sech2(η/6​),J=346​​.​
(137)
Consequently δ=(ρJν2/F)1/3x2/3 and U=[F2/(ρ2J2ν)]1/3x−1/3. The transverse velocity describes entrainment; the profile need not have f(∞)=0 when its axial velocity vanishes there.

39B (Waves)

Words: 330 Articles: 1
Section II OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 330
39B OurBigBook.com
Use an acoustic velocity potential φ with u=∇φ and p′=−ρ0​φt​. It obeys the wave equation φtt​=c02​∇2φ. The rigid walls require zero normal velocity, hence Neumann boundary conditions on the transverse variables. Separation gives
φ=Re{Aei(kx−ωt)cos(my/α)cos(nz/β)},m,n∈{0,1,2,…}.
(138)
Define κmn2​=m2/α2+n2/β2. The dispersion relation, phase velocity and group velocity for positive k,ω are
ω=c0​k2+κmn2​​,c=kω​=c0​1+k2κmn2​​​,cg​=k2+κmn2​​c0​k​=cc02​​.​
(139)
For a dispersive mode, ω(0)=c0​κmn​>0, c decreases from infinity to c0​, and cg​ increases from zero to c0​. The (0,0) mode has ω=c0​k and c=cg​=c0​: it propagates without dispersion.
Let A=π2αβ be the cross-sectional area. The appropriate time and cross-sectional average at fixed x is
⟨h⟩=2πAω​∫02π/ω​∫0πα​∫0πβ​hdzdydt.
(140)
Write Fmn​(y,z) for the product of cosines and Q=A−1∫Fmn2​dydz. Its transverse eigenvalue and wall conditions give ∫∣∇⊥​Fmn​∣2=κmn2​∫Fmn2​ by integration by parts. The kinetic energy density and compressive acoustic energy density are ρ0​∣u∣2/2 and (p′)2/(2ρ0​c02​). Time averaging each squared real oscillation contributes a factor 1/2, so
⟨Ekin​⟩=4ρ0​∣A∣2Q​(k2+κmn2​)=4c02​ρ0​∣A∣2Qω2​=⟨Ecomp​⟩.​
(141)
This holds for every dispersive mode, and also for the zero mode.
For localized smooth initial data, a dispersive mode contains integrals of the form ∫a(k)eit[kV−ω(k)]dk along x=Vt. When 0<V<c0​, a stationary point exists at k∗​=κmn​V/c02​−V2​. It is nondegenerate because ω′′(k)=c0​κmn2​/(k2+κmn2​)3/2>0. The stationary phase method therefore gives an oscillatory amplitude O(t−1/2) for each excited dispersive mode, and for their sum under sufficient mode summability.
At V=c0​, no dispersive mode has a finite stationary wavenumber; with smooth localized data these contributions decay, while the nondispersive right-moving pulse retains its original amplitude. Thus a general disturbance with nonzero zero-mode component has an undiminished O(1) pulse on the sound-speed ray. If that component is absent, this surviving contribution is absent too. For V>c0​, finite propagation speed puts a compactly supported initial disturbance outside this ray for all sufficiently large t, so the field is eventually zero. Rapidly localized, rather than strictly compact, data give a correspondingly negligible tail instead.

40A (Numerical Analysis)

i

Words: 178 Articles: 1
40A OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 178
i OurBigBook.com
Take b to be the vector of fij​ and absorb h−2 into A. Its diagonal entry is −10/(3h2), each axial-neighbour entry is 2/(3h2) and each diagonal-neighbour entry is 1/(6h2). Since these weights agree in both directions, A is a symmetric matrix.
Extend a grid vector u by zero to the whole integer lattice. Let Ea​ contain unordered axial-neighbour pairs and Ed​ unordered diagonal-neighbour pairs. Only finitely many differences involving nonzero values contribute. Each lattice vertex has total neighbour weight 4(2/3)+4(1/6)=10/3, so expanding the squared differences gives
uTAu=−h21​​32​{v,w}∈Ea​∑​(uv​−uw​)2+61​{v,w}∈Ed​∑​(uv​−uw​)2​.​
(142)
It is nonpositive. If it vanishes, every axial difference vanishes. The axial lattice is connected and u is zero outside the finite interior square, forcing u=0. Thus uTAu<0 for every nonzero u: A is negative definite​.
Reordering the grid replaces A by PTAP for a permutation matrix P. This preserves symmetry and the sign of the quadratic form, proving the assertion for any ordering. Multiplying the whole system by h2 merely rescales A by a positive number and has the same conclusions.

ii

Words: 51 Articles: 1
40A OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 51
ii OurBigBook.com
Let D=−10I/(3h2) be the diagonal part of A. The weighted Jacobi method is
u(r+1)=(1−ω)u(r)+ωD−1[b−(A−D)u(r)].​
(143)
Equivalently it is u(r+1)=u(r)+ωD−1(b−Au(r)). In grid form, all neighbours on the right are taken from the old iterate:
uij(r+1)​=(1−ω)uij(r)​+ω​51​axial∑​u(r)+201​diagonal∑​u(r)−103h2​fij​​.​
(144)
The boundary values stay zero at every step. The iteration matrix is Tω​=I−ωD−1A.

iii

Words: 194 Articles: 1
40A OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 194
iii OurBigBook.com
For ω=1, the Jacobi method iteration matrix T=I−D−1A has zero diagonal, nonnegative axial entries 1/5, and diagonal-neighbour entries 1/20. Its row sums are at most one; they are strictly below one at grid points next to the Dirichlet boundary. Its graph is connected by the positive axial entries.
To prove the strict spectral radius bound, let Tz=λz with z=0 and choose a component of maximum magnitude M>0. Then
∣λ∣M≤∑w​Tvw​∣zw​∣≤M∑w​Tvw​≤M,
(145)
so ∣λ∣≤1. If equality held, every positive-weight neighbour of a maximal component would also have modulus M, and that row would have sum one. Propagating along axial edges reaches a boundary-adjacent row, whose sum is strictly less than one, a contradiction. This also covers a one-point interior grid, for which T=0. Hence
ρ(T)<1.​
(146)
The standard convergence theorem for a stationary linear iteration says it converges from every initial vector exactly when its iteration matrix has spectral radius below one. Since A is invertible by (i), the error satisfies e(r)=Tre(0)→0 and
ω=1 converges to the unique solution of Au=b.​
(147)
Weak row diagonal dominance alone would not prove convergence; the connection to a strictly deficient boundary row supplies the required strictness.
